pg:https://www.wral.com/weather/voyager-.desc: Nearly 50 years after launch, Voyager 1 has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, continuing to send scientific data across 16 billion miles
paras: Voyager 1 reaches a milestone nearly 50 years in the making: One light-day from Earth Nearly 50 years after launch, Voyager 1 has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, continuing to send scientific data across 16 billion miles Posted 11/18/2026, 4:12:17 PM By Tony Rice, NASA Ambassador Nearly five decades after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled so far that radios signal take an entire day to reach it and it to reach back out to Earth. No human-made object has ever been this far away.

It crossed the one-light-day milestone.Wednesday morning, November 18, becoming the first human-made object to travel that far from Earth. At 5:16 a.m. Eastern time, the spacecraft passed a distance of 16.094 billion miles, or 25.902 billion kilometers. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. At approximately 186,000 miles per second, that works out to more than 16 billion miles.

A signal weaker than you can imagine Getting data back to Earth from a light day away is engineering accomplishment in itself. By the time Voyager's radio signal reaches Earth, its power has faded to approximately -160 dBm, or about 100 attowatts. An attowatt is one quintillionth of a watt.

Today's Trump-Putin meeting will be closely watched by Ukraine and the rest of Europe, which asserted last week that there could be "no discussions about Ukraine without Ukraine, and no discussions about Europe without Europe".

pg:https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5m.desc: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
paras: In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: The ICJ rules on The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar. Here’s what’s at stake for the Rohingya.
paras: On Thursday, November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its verdict in a landmark case brought by The Gambia, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority.

The ruling, which will be final and cannot be appealed, comes seven years after The Gambia filed its case with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and more than nine years after a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority who have lived for centuries in Rakhine State, western Myanmar.

pg:https://www.nbcnews.com/world/asia/wo.desc: The meeting represents a major shift from Washington’s post-Cold War policy of driving a wedge between Moscow and Beijing.

pg:https://www.dw.com/en/what-the-crimea.desc: Ukraine's latest strike on the Kerch Bridge has disrupted a key transport link between Russia and Crimea. Beyond the damage, the attack could have serious consequences for Russian military logistics and Putin's prestige.

Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.

paras: A key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.

For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

pg:https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/.desc: It's the little space probe that could: Nearly 50 years after it was launched, NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day — or 16 billion miles — away from Earth.
paras: It's the little space probe that could: Nearly 50 years after it was launched, NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day — or 16 billion miles — away from Earth.

Voyager 1 and its sister spacecraft, Voyager 2, set off in 1977 on their mission to explore the solar system's giant planets – Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – and their moons. A rare planetary alignment at the time allowed NASA to chart a flight path that required minimal fuel, using the planets' gravity to slingshot the probes toward their destinations.

The twin spacecraft beamed dazzling, never-before-seen photos of the outer planets back to Earth and revealed many of their secrets for the first time — like the discovery that Jupiter's Great Red Spot is an enormous storm system.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: The US, Chinese and Russian leaders are to hold their first three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
paras: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Manila.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/global-de.desc: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

pg:https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-en.desc: This record-breaking documentary finally arrives on British shores, and it’s every bit as bewitching as you’ve heard
paras: Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

In an interview last week, Lance Oppenheim, co-director of the hit, record-breaking documentary You Can See Everything, described the film’s ostensible subject, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, as a “human optical illusion”. He’s got a point. Throughout You Can See Everything – or at least, throughout the sections in which she appears, filmed mostly in the month leading directly up to her imprisonment – Holmes, moon-eyed and taut-voiced, is a figure of total, mystifying opacity.

Holmes may indeed be the illusion, but she’s not necessarily the illusionist. The heart of You Can See Everything, 2026’s very best film, is a triangle: at one vertex you have Holmes, at another, her current partner, Billy Evans. At the third sits Nathan Fielder, the film’s other director, who spends weeks interviewing the couple, eventually moving in to live with them in the days before Holmes surrenders herself to a Texan prison.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/commentis.desc: I don’t know how the film will make me feel, I assume bad. But I will take the psychic damage. I’ll do it for the culture
paras: I don’t know how the film will make me feel, I assume bad. But I will take the psychic damage. I’ll do it for the culture

I realise it’s only the most annoying people on Earth who say this sort of thing, but I’m going to bravely say it anyway: I am an empath. I have always felt in tune with other people’s emotions and can easily take them on. The emotion I am most intensely attuned to, the one that takes the strongest hold of my body when I see someone going through it? Embarrassment.

There is nothing I hate more than seeing a person embarrassed, even if it’s a person I don’t like. I have always been like this. I remember sitting in the cinema watching There’s Something About Mary, all of my friends dying over a scene where Ben Stiller gets his testicular skin stuck in his zipper in front of his crush. They were rolling in their seats while my insides were rolling around. I felt physically ill. I knew logically it was a funny scene, that a normal person would laugh at the plight of this poor boy and his ball skin, but my humour bone was being crushed in a vice grip, as it always is when embarrassment abounds.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026.desc: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller
paras: Peter BradshawThu 19 Nov 2026 10.00 GMTLast modified on Thu 19 Nov 2026 15.58 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger.

Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here.

What we get is an Olympic stare-out contest between two gladiators of the polite straight face. Fielder’s conversations with the equally pop-eyed Evans have the same tension. Who is going to lose their cool first? Holmes repeatedly insists that the technology works, by which she appears to mean that the technology has caused her to be certain in the present that it could and will work in the future; the theory is impeccable and all that remains is the small matter of getting whatever tech stuff they need to go in the little box.

If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).

But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.

I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable.

pg:http://obernolte.house.gov/media/pres.desc: WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) announced today that his bipartisan Preventive Health Savings Act (H.R. 4464), legislation to modernize how Congress evaluates the long-term fiscal impact of preventive health care policies, has passed the U.S. House of Representatives.
paras: WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) announced today that his bipartisan Preventive Health Savings Act (H.R. 4464), legislation to modernize how Congress evaluates the long-term fiscal impact of preventive health care policies, has passed the U.S. House of Representatives.

Led by Rep. Obernolte and Rep. Diana DeGette (CO-01), the Preventive Health Savings Act will allow the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) to evaluate the potential long-term savings of preventive health care legislation over a 30-year period. Currently, CBO primarily evaluates legislation within a 10-year budget window, which can overlook savings from policies that prevent chronic diseases, reduce the need for costly medical treatments, or improve long-term health outcomes.

By providing Congress with a more complete understanding of the potential long-term savings associated with preventive care, the legislation aims to support evidence-based health care policies that improve patient outcomes while reducing future federal health care expenditures.

pg:https://news.illinois.edu/is-the-proj.desc: Illinois expert addresses the public health impacts of U.S. Army’s planned detonation of lead explosives.
paras: CHAMPAIGN, Ill. ­— On Monday, Nov. 23, the U.S. Army plans to conduct two controlled detonations of degraded lead azide explosives in Middletown, Iowa, generating a plume spreading lead dust across eastern Iowa and western Illinois. Dr. Will Sander, a professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, spoke with News Bureau Biomedical Sciences Editor Liz Ahlberg Touchstone about what the detonation could mean for public health, and what precautions residents can take both during the event and in the aftermath.

There is a mild public health concern, particularly for young children. There is no acceptable level of lead exposure for people, as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and children are much more sensitive to lead due to the potential effects on brain development. Unfortunately, lead does not break down, so there is still some inherent risk no matter how long after the air plume occurs.

People in the potential area of air drift should stay inside as much as possible during the first 24 hours after the explosion to minimize risk. However, you can still go outside for short times as needed to take the dog out or get to the store.

pg:https://eos.org/research-and-developm.desc: Scientists and Iowa residents are planning to independently monitor lead levels in the air and soil in the days before and after a planned detonation of lead azide, a military explosive, near Middletown, Iowa on Monday.
paras: The stockpile of lead azide, held at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, has been deemed unsafe to transport by the U.S. Army. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted an emergency permit to the U.S. Army based on the explosion risk, saying that the condition of the lead azide “presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”

Maps released by the U.S. Army this week showed that a plume of lead-containing dust could travel roughly 100 miles from Middletown in the hours after the detonation. However, new official maps of the plume were not updated following an announcement that the detonation, originally scheduled for Friday, had moved to Monday.

That’s left scientists and communities with just days to make plans to monitor the plume’s impacts. “These are tough circumstances to plan sampling campaigns under,” said University of Iowa environmental scientist David Cwiertny, who is leading an effort to track lead levels in the environment both before and after the detonation. “But we’ll do what we can.”

pg:https://movieweb.com/gta-6-lucia-twis.desc: It was bound to stir up controversy eventually.

Controversy was guaranteed to follow GTA 6, if only due to the franchise it is couched within, but the pushback currently being aimed at one of the lead characters isn't the criticism most people were expecting. Previous games have been torn apart by people who believe they glorify violence, romanticize criminality, and encourage general lawlessness, but that's not the criticism currently swirling around Rockstar's latest release.

A few gamers are instead rankled at the fact that, early in the story, the game's female protagonist displays a heavily questionable parenting choice. One gamer, who goes by @squidlord on X, said they lost interest in GTA 6 after a plot line within the first 30 minutes of gameplay gave them "such a visceral reaction there was no way I was ever going to be back on board to support dealing with them."

The upset these gamers express is interesting, considering its source. It's almost as if they've forgotten what franchise they're playing. For those who've never enjoyed the GTA games, it seems important to point out how extreme some of the storylines within them can get. In GTA 5, for example, there is an unskippable, necessary plot line in which one of the protagonists quite willingly tortures a man for information.

pg:https://www.avclub.com/game-theory-gr.desc: Grand Theft Auto VI and The Game Awards deserve each other
paras: The current reason I’m feeling like a frog slow-boiling in the warm waters of a fictitious, it-took-human-beings-10-million-hours-of-computer-drudgery-to-model Florida city, though, is that other tentpole event sticking out of end of the annual gaming calendar, like a piece of rebar lodged in Phineas Gage’s head: The Game Awards. After all, it was Tuesday morning when Geoff Keighley’s celebration of video game commercials (with the occasional trophy, or dollop of supposed activism, thrown in) announced that GTA VI had been nominated for Game Of The Year, despite, again, the total number of people who’d played it at that point likely not breaking a thousand.

I’m not suggesting any kind of impropriety here, mind you; the critics who voted for the game’s nomination are probably from the major outlets that have played it—and even if they weren’t, I’m open to the idea that Grand Theft Auto VI should have a GOTY nomination locked down from this particular body, basically by default. Because, honestly, GTA and The Game Awards deserve each other.

You can argue, as I imagine Keighley would, that this kind of communal interest is a net benefit to gaming, creating a force of attention so large that not even our collective cultural gatekeepers can deny it. (Because, god, but is there nothing that a certain kind of gaming brain can’t stand then to be casually dismissed by The New York Times.) Meanwhile, those of us on the skeptic side can point to all the ways the TGAs do what monocultures always do, i.e., grind down massive amounts of diversity and varied experiences into a uniform nubbin while extracting as much cash from folks as humanly possible.

But I believe it’s way more likely that they are starting again as though nothing has happened, like it’s a multiverse in a Marvel movie where old or dead or alternate versions of superheroes just turn up and do their thing.”

Questions had been asked before over the future of the Bond character, particularly after it was revealed in the run-up to No Time to Die in 2019 that the 007 codename was to be given to Lashana Lynch’s new MI6 agent Nomi. Was Bond really about to be put out to pasture? The ambiguity of the future of Bond – which was seen by some as a new front in the culture war – was underscored by Craig’s open dislike of the role, and his determination that No Time to Die was his last film in the role.

Vaines suggests that the Bond death narrative was Craig’s way of making sure he never had to come back to a series that, at that time, was still under the control of its original production company Eon. “I believe Daniel Craig wanted a definitive line drawn under his Bond, which everyone agreed on at the time. The Eon team may well have just planned to effectively start again the way that rather good opening sequence in the first Craig Bond played out, establishing after two kills that he was an 00 agent. paras: Climate talks have gone into extra time at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Türkiye, after almost 200 nations couldn’t reach a consensus on a final deal, as disagreements over fossil fuels and climate finance hobbled efforts.
The row escalated after a revised draft text, issued on Thursday, omitted mentions of phasing out coal, oil and gas, prompting protests from European and developing countries.

France, Panama, and other countries demanded unequivocal words on ending fossil fuels. “The talks are still savable,” said Panama Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro, adding there was time to get tough on ending fossil fuels.

pg:https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c.desc: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
paras: Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026.desc: Rodrigo Muniz set Fulham on the way but Elliot Anderson volley earns Manchester City a valuable Premier League point.

Anderson’s driven volley from the edge of the box in the 57th minute handed City their first point in the league since they opened their campaign with seven consecutive wins.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/technolog.desc: Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve the math problem involving prime numbers
paras: A mathematician at Anthropic is contending that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

If Alpöge’s claim is ultimately confirmed, the proof could mark another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

pg:https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/21/tech/a.desc: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company’s AI tool Claude.

paras: New Delhi: Negotiations at the UN climate summit in Turkey extended into “extra time” on Saturday, as consensus on the outcome document remained elusive amid deep divisions among nations over how the text should address fossil fuel emissions in an increasingly warming world, while also taking into account the Global South’s demand for economic growth.

Negotiators worked through the night to try to break the deadlock over energy, finance and science, as the summit went past its scheduled closing time on Friday without an agreement. Saudi Arabia, Russia and India are among the countries understood to have opposed any decisive reference to the “phase-out of fossil fuels” in the text.

From the outset of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, references to fossil fuels remained central to the deadlock, pushing the summit into overtime.

Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.

pg:https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-.desc: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
paras: A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, delaying an agreement at the two-week conference that had been scheduled to end on Friday.

pg:https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ri.desc: The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
paras: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

Myanmar's government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court's demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.

paras: Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

paras: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31, has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years.

The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years.

But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot”. Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through.

pg:https://time.com/article/2026/11/23/c.desc: Don't confuse the lack of another global accord with the lack of international engagement to tackle climate change.
paras: Participants sleep under COP31 signage in the main hall on the final day of the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference on Nov. 20 in Antalya, Turkey.

In the eleven years since the Paris Agreement, countries around the world have met annually to plot out the global consensus on how to tackle climate change. In some years negotiations led to big breakthroughs. In others, talks simply kept the ball in play, signaling to the world that nations were aligned in their desire to tackle climate change, even if it’s hard to agree on the exact path forward.

So it was a striking moment in the three-decade arc of United Nations climate negotiations when talks fell apart in Turkey over the weekend at this year’s COP31. The decade-long global consensus about the urgency of tackling climate change that produced the Paris Agreement at COP21 in 2015, it seems, came to an end on Sunday. The issues at play were many, of various levels of complexity, but the biggest was rather simple: a group of countries led by Saudi Arabia and Russia resisted reference to phasing out fossil fuels in the final text, and a bloc of 130 countries including the European Union refused to sign on without it.

paras: Add Defector to Google 131CommentsI did not imagine that the release of Grand Theft Auto VI would have any meaningful impact on my life, for the simple reason that I am not a gamer. I know and even respect a few people for whom video games are important, but I mainly regard this in the same way I do friends who really like square dancing, or go to church: nice for them, but not really my business.

I watched clips of people doing things Lucia will appreciate: buying groceries, taking her shopping, picking up flowers. pg:https://www.dw.com/en/cop-deadlock-pr.desc: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?
paras: After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

paras: It hasn't happened since 2009: International talks to fight climate change ended without any new pledges and commitments.

The summit, held this year in Antalya, Turkey, and known as COP31, was overshadowed by geopolitical tensions and wars, the withdrawal of U.S. President Donald Trump from the United Nations process to tackle climate change and growing alarm over the accelerating pace of global warming.

On Sunday, with the faltering talks already in overtime, the EU delegation walked out of the negotiations and said it could not accept a final declaration that did include language over the need to transition away from fossil fuels. The United Kingdom and many developing nations also rejected the proposed text as unacceptable.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/20.desc: The failure exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
paras: COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.

It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.

Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.

But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for a historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

pg:https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/cop31-t.desc: Climate talks collapsed on Sunday at COP31 in Turkey, ending the longest ever United Nations climate summit with no deal to show for it.
paras: For more than two weeks, representatives from nearly 200 countries, scientists, businesses and more gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for this year's COP31 conference.

The annual UN Climate Change Conference brings together member states to negotiate — and ideally commit to — climate policies that aim to curb global warming. It's the main vehicle through which countries co-ordinate climate action.

But this year, no agreement was reached — despite extending heavily into overtime this weekend following Friday's deadline — after the European Union and others rejected the draft put forward by Turkey and Australia.

paras: The full moon will reach peak illumination at 9:54 a.m. ET tomorrow, according to EarthSky. While that peak occurs during daylight hours in the United States, the lunar orb will still appear full tonight, as well as Tuesday and Wednesday evening, said Noah Petro, chief of NASA’s Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Lab at Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.
November’s full moon is known as the beaver moon — a nod to the time of year when the industrious dam-building mammals prepare for winter. The event will be the first of three consecutive supermoons.

November’s full moon will appear about 17% larger and 30% brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, Petro said. “Folks who pay regular attention to full moons will notice the difference,” he added.

In the outer solar system, icy bodies are spread widely beyond Neptune. Many are concentrated in the Kuiper Belt, about 38–50 astronomical units (AU; 1 AU is the average Earth–Sun distance of about 150 million km) from the Sun. The problem is that over the past two decades, objects with highly elongated or steeply inclined orbits have been discovered much farther out. It has been pointed out that the gravity of known planets, including Neptune, alone cannot easily explain their movements.

A representative case is Sedna. This body travels around the Sun on a long, elliptical orbit and stays far beyond Neptune's orbit even at its closest approach to the Sun. The gravity of known planets alone cannot easily explain how such an orbit formed. An alternative hypothesis to explain this is "Planet Nine," a hidden giant planet with 5–10 times Earth's mass.

paras: NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year's U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year's summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year's climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world's richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

pg:https://www.thecut.com/article/jensen.desc: For his return to Nvidia, Huang ditched his signature black leather in favor of navy cotton.
paras: If you can get past how wild it is that Huang’s Nvidia employees are acting like he just returned from war (he was gone for 11 days), you’ll notice that his jacket appears to be cotton. Clearly, Huang thought that the working man’s fabric would look best as he held his hand to his heart and expressed his gratitude. Black leather would be too flashy for the occasion, but navy cotton? That has just the right amount of humility. That’s a jacket that says, “I’m listening and learning.”

Huang’s “man of the people” jacket looks a lot like one he wore in June during a trip to Seoul. Perhaps he was hoping to show how down to earth he can be by shopping his own closet? Photos from the trip give us a clearer image of the chest logo, which is, of course, Dior. In fact, this is not even a jacket at all — it’s described on the label’s website as a “zipped shirt.” How much will a Dior zipped shirt cost a simple man who just wants to get back to work? $3,300 — a steal!

I doubt Huang will be able to deny the siren song of his signature look for too long. By next week, I imagine he’ll be back to his pre-scandal lifestyle: leather jackets, 14-hour workdays, and preaching the gospel of AI. Hopefully there will be fewer affairs this time around.

Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games. It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release.

When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post, that is 3.8%.

Markle was arrested in early November after federal officials say they found dozens of illicit images, including film negatives, slides and books depicting suspected child abuse, in a storage facility in Los Angeles. Court filings also allege Markle possessed similar material in the Philippines, where he has a home and where some of the lewd photos of the children appear to have been taken. Markle himself was identified by a witness in at least two photos with a nude, prepubescent girl, according to the indictment.
Markle is currently in jail in Florida, where he was arrested November 6 at a senior living facility, but he will be transferred to Los Angeles in the coming weeks, Essayli’s office wrote.

pg:https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/.desc: Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 mass shooting that claimed 13 lives, is set to be executed on Dec. 3, but a new filing could lead to a significant delay.
paras: Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed 13 lives, filed a motion for a stay of execution so he can submit what’s known as a habeas corpus petition, which requires the government to justify a person’s detainment.
Hasan, 56, had officially exhausted his military justice appeals, opening the door to President Donald Trump in October approving his death sentence and the Army setting an execution date.

Hasan’s request was filed in civilian court, which is another process available to military prisoners. Military experts told NBC News the legal maneuver to file a habeas corpus petition would all but assure Hasan’s case will be tied up in a lengthy review process that could effectively stall his pending execution to well beyond the end of Trump’s term. At that point, they say, Trump’s successor may avoid setting another execution date.

pg:https://gizmodo.com/grand-theft-auto-.desc: Finding it only took three days of grinding.
paras: Given that half the world has been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since its release last Thursday, it’s no surprise that the game’s secrets and Easter eggs are being cracked in record time. Perhaps the most impressive discovery so far is a secret cracked by a player named Memeio, who tweeted that he had spent three days going further and further down a rabbit hole that led him to a portal into… Grand Theft Auto Vice City, circa 2002.

The discovery is another entry in the rich tradition of secrets that return players to earlier entries in a given series. My personal favorite is the various secret levels in the 2016 reboot of Doom, which allowed players to revisit levels from the original 1993 Doom, complete with original graphics, music and sound effects. The GTA VI secret does something similar, but—befitting a game with a 10-figure budget—it takes the idea a step further, also bringing back one of the voice actors from the 2002 game.

The GTA VI secret is hidden behind an awfully convoluted multi-faceted puzzle involving the game’s power stations. Memeio’s video catalogs the sequence of steps needed to solve that puzzle, and… well, you can see why it took him three days of grinding to figure it out.

Consider, when surveying not just the game that it ended up being, but the work that went into making it, that multiple things can be true about Grand Theft Auto VI at once. Like:

Do I, personally, find the actions of Rockstar management abhorrent? Absolutely, and I fully support the affected workers (and the union itself) in their ongoing efforts. But do I also appreciate the work that has gone into this astounding video game, the craft and love and joy that has gone into every NPC interaction, every in-universe radio show and every industry-accurate piece of Florida infrastructure? The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes.
On Tuesday, the army released new maps forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/football/.desc: Raheem Sterling has avoided jail, receiving a 12 month sentence suspended for 18 months at Basingstoke magistrates court
paras: Raheem Sterling has avoided jail for dangerous driving while inhaling nitrous oxide, receiving a 12-month sentence suspended for 18 months at Basingstoke magistrates court on Wednesday.

The former England international was also ordered to do 100 hours of community service. His MBE and charitable and foundation work was accepted in mitigation, together with his decision to voluntarily submit to addiction treatment.
Sterling pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving after driving his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide in May.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

pg:https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/sci.desc: Beaver Supermoon 2026 explained: what it is, why November’s moon appears larger, and when the next supermoons will occur.
paras: The full supermoon, also known as the Beaver Moon, rises behind the Chrysler Building and the Manhattan skyline as a helicopter flies past in New York City, US, November 24, 2026. | Photo Credit: REUTERS

Skywatchers were treated to a dazzling view as the Beaver Supermoon lit up the night skies on Tuesday (November 24, 2026). The November full moon, known as the Beaver Moon, appears larger and brighter than usual due to its proximity to Earth. Here is more about the celestial display and when you can watch the next supermoon

The moon revolves around the Earth in an oval-shaped path (elliptical orbit). A supermoon occurs when the moon rises near perigee (the point in its orbit closest to earth), appearing larger and brighter than usual. This year’s full moon (November 24) is known as the Beaver Supermoon because this is when beavers prepare for the winter and also the time of year to set beaver traps before the swamps and rivers froze.

pg:https://www.cbsnews.com/news/china-la.desc: China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts, sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.
paras: China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2.desc: Divers recover bodies after Cessna 210 went down in Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday afternoon killing all onboard
paras: Divers have found the bodies of six people killed in a small plane crash on Tuesday off the coast of Mississippi, according to the US Coast Guard.

Their bodies were in the plane’s fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands national seashore. Four adults and two boys, ages eight and 10, were onboard, a Coast Guard spokesperson, Juan Ros, said.

The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported about 3.45pm that it lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. Responders searched for hours and initially only found three lifejackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.

pg:https://www.npr.org/2026/11/25/g-s1-1.desc: Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius to prepare to dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide. And, after a nearly two-year legal battle, Kilmar Abrego Garcia's has voluntarily left the U.S.
paras: The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-ra.desc: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions
paras: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions

Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband.

Since it is ultimately about the video fragments in our minds, Blade Runner has, from the start, presented its conception of the future as more of a mood than a story. One of the many things Blade Runner 2099 creator/writer Silka Luisa gets right is keeping that allusive wooziness, prioritising images over details and vibes over the desire to build a complete, logically functioning world. It’s important to, uh, remember that before diving in.

pg:https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/us-spai.desc: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the U.S., arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
paras: Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to an El Salvador prison despite never having been convicted of a crime in the U.S.

Protracted legal battles ensued. A judge accused U.S. President Donald Trump's administration of "bad faith" when it said it was helpless to adhere a court order to return him from the notorious CECOT prison to the U.S.
Abrego Garcia was only returned in June 2025 when federal officials charged him with a series of offences including human smuggling in relation to a 2022 incident in Tennessee.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: The US is planning tariffs on 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their industries overproduce.
paras: The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.

A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2.desc: Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%
paras: Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.

Video showed that the nearly 4,500kg (10,000lb) of lead azide – a highly volatile, lead-based explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I – was detonated in two successive open-air detonations on Wednesday at around 9am (15:00 GMT).

paras: Nvidia’s board faces scrutiny after unanimously rehiring Jensen Huang days after accepting his resignation, fuelling calls for accountability and transparency.

NEW YORK: Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company's board is joining him at the centre of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia's president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and "input from senior levels of the United States government". paras: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.

A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.

The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.

pg:https://www.politico.eu/article/cop-i.desc: The chaotic conclusion of the COP31 conference is turning nations against the process.

Rifts proved so fractious at the talks in Antalya, Turkey, that governments could not seal a high-level deal for the first time since 2009. pg:https://www.theguardian.com/commentis.desc: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again, says author and journalist Natalie Morris
paras: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again

When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity.

Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday. But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes.

A statement from Duran Duran added: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

The following month Simon Le Bon joined as frontman, by February 1981 they had released their debut single Planet Earth, and with the July release of Girls on Film – a song propelled by Taylor’s ultra-tight and rhythmic playing – they became major stars in the UK and US. Rio, their second album released in 1982, cemented their international playboy image and went Top 10 in both countries, and follow-up Seven and the Ragged Tiger topped the UK chart. With their new game, Grand Theft Auto VI, they have slowed things down even more. There are still, to be sure, plenty of sequences featuring the high-octane action the series is known for. But it’s the game’s banality that seems to be sticking with players just as much. In between missions featuring gunfights, police chases and robberies, players spend just as much time on activities that are entirely mundane. In a genre – a medium, even – so committed to constant stimulation of your dopamine receptors, Grand Theft Auto VI manages to be most engaging when you’re forced to take your time.

But Grand Theft Auto 6 specifically focuses on the systemic issues that make any version of the American Dream — saving money, buying a home and supporting a family with a fulfilling job — incredibly difficult for people living on the margins of society. The crushing weight of capitalism is always pressing down on you, just like in the real world.

Lucia Caminos committed an ill-conceived robbery, is subsequently sent to jail and is forced to claw her way back into civilian life with little support. Jason Duval joined the Army to escape his troubled youth and ends up serving as muscle for a small-time criminal. Much like the real Bonnie and Clyde, Lucia and Jason are driven by the need to escape poverty, but it's up to you to determine if they'll share a similar end.

I only have around 12 hours of GTA 6 under my belt so far (it's estimated to take around 50 hours to beat, and hundreds of hours to fully complete), but Rockstar clearly frames why our lead characters pursue a life of crime: beyond the generational poverty and lack of upward mobility, Lucia and Jason are also trying to build enough stability to reclaim custody of their infant son.

pg:https://finance.biggo.com/news/6012b2.desc: The European Space Agency's Hera probe has delivered the first close-up look at Dimorphos since NASA's DART spacecraft struck it in 2022, finding that…
paras: Hera, which launched in October 2024 and arrived at the binary asteroid system on Nov. 4, has found that the face of Dimorphos struck by DART was compressed into an impact basin roughly the size of a sports stadium and stretching across the asteroid's full width. The 2022 collision also appears to have altered the body's overall shape and left it rotating erratically.

The findings were released alongside the first batch of close-up imagery, presented during a live broadcast on Wednesday, giving the public its first detailed look at the crash site since the Double Asteroid Redirection Test struck on Sept. 26, 2022.

DART was designed as a planetary defense experiment: a deliberate, high-speed collision to test whether humanity could nudge a threatening space rock off course. The target, Dimorphos, is a small moonlet orbiting the larger asteroid Didymos. The spacecraft hit at roughly 14,000 miles per hour (about 22,500 kilometers per hour), throwing a plume of debris into space and shortening the moonlet's orbital period around Didymos by about 33 minutes.

pg:https://www.popsci.com/science/dart-m.desc: The ESA's first detailed images of Dimorphos are here.
paras: Add Popular Science (opens in a new tab) After over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from ESA’s Hera spacecraft highlight the results of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test’s (DART) intentional run-in with Didymos’ 500-foot-wide moonlet Dimorphos in 2022, revealing a stadium-sized crater, cloud of boulders, and a new, erratic orbital path.

Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings.
Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera.
